prohibited_recommendations: Do not perform the large-volume lumbar tap before brain MRI has excluded a recurrent subdural collection, a mass or obstructive hydrocephalus
Do not perform the lumbar tap while rivaroxaban is active and do not bridge with heparin [ASRA_2025] [ACCP_2022]
Do not label the hydrocephalus idiopathic: the subdural haematomas and their evacuation are an antecedent, which makes it secondary normal pressure hydrocephalus
Do not attribute the syndrome to normal ageing or deconditioning once the ventriculomegaly and the tap response are documented
required_recommendations: Refer to neurosurgery for CSF shunting for secondary normal pressure hydrocephalus after the bilateral subdural haematomas, with a programmable valve given the risk of a recurrent subdural collection with overdrainage, on the basis of the tap-test improvement of 31% in TUG at 24 hours, the supportive MRI and normal-pressure CSF [Nakajima_2021]

Hold rivaroxaban for at least 72 hours before the lumbar tap and restart it no sooner than 24 hours after, without heparin bridging, weighing the interruption against the stroke risk of atrial fibrillation [ASRA_2025] [ACCP_2022]
Falls-prevention measures (physiotherapy, home assessment, walking aid) while awaiting surgery

avoided_actions.rationale: He has no episodes suggesting seizures after the burr-hole surgery, so an EEG does not inform the gait work-up.
His atrial fibrillation is already known and anticoagulated and the falls are not syncopal, so an ECG adds nothing to the work-up.
There is no syncope, murmur or embolic event, so echocardiography has no role in this work-up.
An MRI is available and excludes a recurrent subdural collection and measures the callosal angle and temporal horns better than CT.
Atrial fibrillation is already documented and anticoagulated, so rhythm monitoring adds nothing to the gait work-up.
Molecular or advanced imaging does not change the shunt decision, which rests on MRI and the tap test
A full neuropsychological battery is not needed for the shunt decision; the bedside screen and timed gait measures are
Normal-pressure CSF with a normal cell count in a chronic afebrile gait syndrome gives no indication for prion, inflammatory or infectious assays.

accepted: Secondary normal pressure hydrocephalus, post-subdural haematoma evacuation

differential.key_features: The ventricles enlarged after the 6-month post-operative CT that followed bilateral subdural haematomas and their evacuation, an antecedent that makes the hydrocephalus secondary rather than idiopathic.
Recurrence is the first concern in an anticoagulated man after burr-hole evacuation, but the MRI shows no residual or recurrent collection.

differential.diagnosis: Vascular cognitive impairment / progressive small-vessel ischaemic disease
differential.key_features: White matter change is only Fazekas grade 1 and there is no infarct, too little to explain the decline.
Normal tone, no tremor or bradykinesia, and a gait that improved after CSF removal argue against parkinsonism.
Free recall normalises with cues, the hippocampi are MTA 1 and the decline followed the hydrocephalus, which does not suggest Alzheimer's disease.

differential.diagnosis: Cerebral atrophy with secondary ex-vacuo ventriculomegaly
differential.key_features: Ventricles out of proportion to the sulci, an acute callosal angle, enlarged temporal horns and a 31% tap response argue against atrophy ex vacuo.

key_clinical_evidence: After a good recovery from bilateral chronic subdural haematoma evacuation, a new 8-month decline in gait, cognition and continence with ventricles that enlarged after the 6-month post-operative CT is secondary normal pressure hydrocephalus, not iNPH [Nakajima_2021]
MRI shows Evans index 0.36 with an acute callosal angle (78 degrees), temporal horns out of proportion to the hippocampi and a patent aqueduct, and no residual or recurrent subdural collection
Opening pressure 17 cmH2O with normal CSF content; after 45 mL was removed, TUG improved 31% at 24 hours (26 to 18 s) and the 10-metre walk 28% [Nakajima_2021]
Tap-test sensitivity is 26% to 61% with a PPV of 73% to 100% [Marmarou_2005]
Secondary NPH is treated by the same shunt route as iNPH; a programmable valve lets the setting be raised if a subdural collection recurs with overdrainage [Nakajima_2021]
Rivaroxaban must be held for at least 72 hours before the neuraxial puncture and restarted no sooner than 24 hours after, without heparin bridging (CHA2DS2-VASc 2) [ASRA_2025] [ACCP_2022]

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: The MRI shows no residual or recurrent subdural collection; the delayed decline comes from the communicating hydrocephalus that followed the haematomas, as the ventricles enlarged after the 6-month CT and the gait improved after CSF removal.
red_herrings.data_point: Chronic subdural hematoma (bilateral, evacuated 14 months ago)
red_herrings.intended_effect: The new gait and cognitive decline is attributed to a recurrent subdural haematoma, or the hydrocephalus is called idiopathic

sequence_constraints.reason: Brain imaging must exclude a mass or obstructive hydrocephalus before CSF is removed [Relkin_2005]
The baseline gait must be measured before the tap, or the post-tap change cannot be interpreted [Nakajima_2021]
The timed gait is repeated after the tap, at 2 to 24 hours, so that its change from the baseline measures the response to CSF removal [Nakajima_2021]

patient.chief_complaint: Progressive gait deterioration and mild cognitive decline 14 months after bilateral subdural hematoma evacuation

past_medical_history: Chronic subdural hematoma (bilateral, evacuated 14 months ago)

patient.history_present_illness: A 74-year-old right-handed man with hypertension, atrial fibrillation, and bilateral chronic subdural hematomas (surgically evacuated 14 months ago via bilateral burr holes) was admitted for evaluation of a gait and cognitive decline. Post-operatively following his subdural evacuation, he had an acceptable recovery — cognitive function improved and he was ambulatory without assistance. However, over the past 8 months his gait has progressively deteriorated with increasing shuffling, wide-based gait, and two falls. He requires a walker. Cognitive performance has also declined gradually, though he remains able to manage daily activities with his wife's assistance. He has developed urinary urgency with occasional incontinence. His neurosurgical team has been following him and reports that a surveillance head CT last month showed enlarged ventricles, which had not been present on the 6-month post-operative CT; the images are not available.
